tldr: In VLA policies for humanoid dual-arm manipulation, this study reveals that a robot's initial configuration introduces a strong bias in hand choice (a policy-induced hand prior). The authors demonstrate that diversifying poses during data collection and intervening on specific arm joints can eliminate this dependence.
hero_caption: Comparison of initial-pose design in training data. Under conventional setups on the left, object locations and initial poses were implicitly coupled. On the right, diversifying arm heights and wrist orientations so that both left and right objects are manipulated from any pose dramatically mitigates excessive dependence on initial pose.
overview:
Recently, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that connect images, language, and actions end-to-end have attracted significant attention. However, even models boasting high benchmark success rates can fail drastically when the robot arm's initial pose changes slightly. In dual-arm robots like humanoids, where the robot must select the right or left hand appropriately based on object position, taking a specific initial pose can trigger bizarre shortcut behaviors—such as reaching out with the right hand even when the object is on the left.

This study defines this initial-condition-driven skew in hand selection as a "policy-induced hand prior" and thoroughly investigates its underlying mechanisms. First, the authors introduce "HandPriorScore," an evaluation metric that compares early left-versus-right hand movement to quantify residual hand bias and target responsiveness. Furthermore, through counterfactual joint-swapping interventions on specific initial poses and wrist-camera masking analyses, they pinpoint which arm joints are responsible for these failures.

Experiments reveal that inappropriate hand selection under certain initial poses is heavily governed by two specific right-arm joint angles ($R_{\mathrm{arm},3}$ and $R_{\mathrm{arm},5}$). In addition, diversifying the initial poses in the training data from 2 to 8 and adding targeted data around weak configurations substantially increases success rates. This paper provides practical insights for diagnosing and resolving initial-pose dependence that often remains hidden behind aggregate benchmark success rates.
contributions: Formulated the "policy-induced hand prior" phenomenon where initial pose causes inappropriate hand selection in dual-arm humanoid VLA manipulation, and proposed the "HandPriorScore" metric based on relative joint displacement.

Identified a causal relationship via joint-level counterfactual intervention experiments, showing that initial angles of specific arm joints ($R_{\mathrm{arm},3}$, $R_{\mathrm{arm},5}$) directly trigger hand-selection switches.
Revealed through presence/absence and masking analyses of wrist cameras that while wrist views support fine-grained motion adjustments, they are not the root cause of incorrect hand selection.

Significantly improved robustness to initial configurations (e.g., from 30% to 75% on a specific pose) by diversifying initial poses and performing targeted data augmentation around failure-prone poses.

sections.heading: Why does a robot get tripped up by its initial pose?
sections.summary: Even when a VLA policy achieves high average task success, differences in initial pose can cause catastrophic failures in specific configurations. In dual-arm humanoids, hand-selection biases emerge where the robot reaches with its right hand even when the object is on the left. This study defines this issue as a policy-induced hand prior and investigates its causes and remedies.
sections.details:
Recent foundation models and VLA policies aim to learn generalist robotic manipulation from large-scale data. However, most existing evaluation protocols begin rollouts from aligned canonical poses or fixed initial positions. This setup overlooks whether the model has overfitted to specific initial configurations.

In practice, variations in initial pose simultaneously alter not only the robot's proprioception, but also how its own arms appear in head-camera views, as well as the geometric relationship between wrist cameras and target objects. Prior work has highlighted shortcut learning, where robots rely too heavily on easy-to-use proprioceptive signals during training while neglecting visual cues.

Preliminary experiments applying GR00T to the Unitree G1 humanoid confirmed that, despite identical object positions, starting from a specific initial pose caused the robot to unnaturally persist in reaching with its right hand toward an apple on the left (wrong-hand choice). To address this, the paper pursues answers to three questions:

- Can altering specific arm joint angles reverse or eliminate this hand bias?
- How do visual observations from wrist cameras influence hand selection and task success?
- How should pose coverage and dataset composition be structured in training data to achieve robustness across initial poses?

sections.heading: VLA robustness and the pitfall of state overfitting
sections.summary: While benchmark evaluations of VLA robustness report performance drops under viewpoint and initial-position perturbations, how these lead to behavioral failures like dual-arm hand misselection has remained unclear. Studies also point to modality imbalances where policies over-rely on internal proprioception over visual inputs. This work delves into how initial pose serves as a shortcut for incorrect action selection.
sections.details:
Related work relevant to this paper falls broadly into two lines of research:

- **VLA policies and robustness under perturbations**
Benchmarks such as LIBERO evaluate general manipulation capabilities, but they predominantly use fixed initial configurations. While perturbation benchmarks like LIBERO-Plus show success drops under shifts in camera view or initial states, they have not probed the behavioral mechanisms explaining why an initial state leads to shortcut behaviors or wrong-hand selection.

- **Vision vs. proprioception bias and state shortcuts**
In multimodal policy learning, proprioceptive signals provide compact, easily predictable cues, which can suppress the learning of visual features (a phenomenon highlighted in GAP and ReViP). Overfitting to state representations in absolute coordinates has also been shown to harm spatial generalization (e.g., State-free Policy).

Building on these findings, this study represents a new effort to diagnose and mitigate how initial pose is learned as a shortcut for hand selection in high-degree-of-freedom dual-arm humanoids where bilateral coordination is critical.

sections.heading: Uncovering hand bias: How HandPriorScore works
sections.summary: To quantify which hand the robot prioritizes right after starting an action, the authors introduce HandPriorScore based on relative joint displacement. This enables decoupling initial-pose-specific hand bias from target responsiveness, independently of object location factors.
sections.details:
The authors formalize a metric to quantify which arm the robot actively uses during the initial decision window (the first $T$ steps) before grasping an object.

### Normalizing relative actions and computing activity
The relative action $\Delta a_{S,t,j}^{G} = a_{S,t,j}^{G} - q_{S,t,j}^{G}$ is computed as the difference between the absolute target joint position $a_{S,t,j}^{G}$ output by the policy and the current joint position $q_{S,t,j}^{G}$ ($S \in \{L, R\}$ indicates the left/right arm and hand, $G \in \{\mathrm{arm}, \mathrm{hand}\}$ indicates the group, and $j$ is the joint index). Because joints have different ranges and variances, relative actions are normalized by the standard deviation $\sigma_{S,j}^{G}$ computed across all evaluation runs, and the root-mean-square (RMS) is taken to calculate motion magnitude $M_{S,t}^{G}$ for each group.

Arm and hand motion magnitudes are combined using weight $\lambda$ to determine aggregate activity $A_{S}^{(T)}$ for each side. The normalized HandPriorScore $H^{(T)}$ is then defined as the difference between left and right activity divided by total activity. A positive value indicates a right-hand preference, while a negative value indicates a left-hand preference.

### Separating hand bias from target responsiveness
By computing the mean score $\mu_{x}^{(T)}$ for each object position (left $\ell$, center $c$, right $r$), the behavior is decomposed into two metrics:

- **Residual hand bias ($H_{\mathrm{prior}}^{(T)}$)**: Calculated as $\frac{1}{2}(\mu_{\ell}^{(T)} + \mu_{r}^{(T)})$, reflecting the intrinsic bilateral bias of the initial pose that remains regardless of whether the target is on the left or right.
- **Target responsiveness ($H_{\mathrm{target}}^{(T)}$)**: Defined as $\frac{1}{2}(\mu_{r}^{(T)} - \mu_{\ell}^{(T)})$, indicating how effectively the robot shifts its hand movements toward the right when the target object moves from left to right.

sections.heading: Experimental setup: The PickApple task on Unitree G1 across 17 initial poses
sections.summary: Experiments were conducted on the dual-arm humanoid Unitree G1 in a PickApple task, where the robot grasps an apple on a table and places it into a tray. Multiple training configurations were designed—including simulation data expanding initial poses from 2 to 8, as well as real-robot data—and closed-loop rollouts were evaluated across 17 initial configurations.
sections.details:
### Datasets and training configurations
The evaluation uses the "PickApple" task, which requires intelligent hand selection based on object position. GR00T-N1.5-3B is used as the base model and fine-tuned.

- **$P_{\mathrm{sim}}$ (simulation data)**: 304 episodes collected across 8 initial poses (pose01–08) varying arm heights and wrist angles, picking and transporting apples placed on either the left or right.
- **Real-robot data**: Combinations of Unitree G1 teleoperated data (single PickApple real dataset $P_{\mathrm{real}}$, a 7-task picking suite, and a 13-task suite including wrist cameras).
- **Training configurations (Table II)**: Simulation-only (Group A), sim plus real-robot data (Group B), wrist cameras enabled (Group C), and simulation reweighted to roughly 45.5% sampling ratio (Groups D and E) to compare the impact of modalities and data mixture ratios.

### Evaluation protocol and 17 initial poses
In addition to the 8 training poses, the authors evaluated 17 initial configurations in total (Fig. 3): the mean of training poses (pose_mean), all joints zeroed (zero), the pre-diversification teleoperation default (teleop_default), starting poses from real-world data (left_real, right_real), and an unseen pose extrapolated in PCA space (synthetic_unseen). Each condition was tested over 20 rollout episodes, strictly scored by a criteria sequence: picking the apple, placing it onto the pink plate, and lifting the arm.

captions.F3: All 17 initial poses used for evaluation alongside initial state distributions for each task, plotted in PCA space. Blue diamonds represent diversified training poses (pose01–08) and blue circles denote additional evaluation poses, demonstrating that robustness is assessed across a broad configuration space.

sections.heading: Results: Strong pose-policy interactions and remarkable joint-level interventions
sections.summary: Success rates on the exact same initial pose varied wildly from 15% to 95% depending on the policy, while a single policy also showed large performance swings across poses. In particular, teleop_default induced a strong right-hand bias; however, swapping just two joint angles on the right arm with values from another pose completely eliminated the wrong-hand selection.
sections.details:
### Initial-pose--policy interactions and hand bias
Experimental results (Fig. 2) highlighted pose-specific failures obscured by aggregate averages. For example, Policy A1 achieved a solid overall average of 61.5%, yet plummeted to 30% on right_real. Furthermore, on teleop_default, the robot frequently forced its right hand toward left-side apples, yielding a large positive residual hand bias $H_{\mathrm{prior}}^{(T)}$.

### Impact of pose diversification and targeted additions
Diversifying initial poses during training from 2 to 8 dramatically boosted average success rates from 5.8% to 63.3% for A1, and from 14.2% to 72.5% for A2 (Fig. 4). Moreover, adding 2 collection poses around the difficult right_real pose (expanding to 10 poses) doubled its success rate on right_real from 30% to 75% (Fig. 5). This confirms that localized gaps in data coverage were the primary driver of failure.

### Role of wrist cameras and auxiliary data
Adding wrist cameras raised overall success from 61.5% (A1) to 76.8% (A2). However, on teleop_default, having wrist cameras ironically reinforced overconfidence in the right hand, increasing wrong-hand attempts on left targets from 6% to 33%. In addition, naively mixing heterogeneous real-robot tasks diluted the target task's data ratio, worsening sensitivity to initial poses.

### Joint-level intervention experiments (Table III, Fig. 7)
To investigate why teleop_default excessively favored the right hand, counterfactual experiments swapped right-arm joint values with right_sim, a similar pose that does not exhibit right-hand bias. Swapping only the two joints with the largest discrepancies—joint 3 ($R_{\mathrm{arm},3}$) and joint 5 ($R_{\mathrm{arm},5}$)—from teleop_default to right_sim values completely eliminated right-hand attempts on left targets (from 7/8 down to 0/4). Conversely, swapping joints with minimal differences ($R_{\mathrm{arm},0}$, $R_{\mathrm{arm},6}$) produced no change. This demonstrates that the policy exploited specific joint angles as shortcuts triggering right-hand usage.

captions.F2: Heatmaps of task success rate (a), residual hand bias (b), and target responsiveness (c) across all 17 initial poses and policies. In specific configurations such as teleop_default, dark red residual bias highlights that hand selection is heavily dominated by initial pose.
captions.F5: Targeted data augmentation around the vulnerable right_real pose (a, b) and its effect (c). Adding just two initial-pose data points along the PC1 axis dramatically improved the success rate on that configuration from 30% to 75%.
captions.F7: Conceptual diagram of joint intervention experiments in PCA space. Swapping the right-arm joints with the largest differences ($R_{\mathrm{arm},3}$, $R_{\mathrm{arm},5}$) between teleop_default and right_sim proves a causal link that substantially suppresses or induces hand bias.
captions.F6: Masking analysis of wrist cameras on teleop_default. Masking wrist images does not produce large shifts in absolute joint output tokens, but clear variations emerge in state-relative fine actions (action_delta_chunk), indicating wrist cameras handle fine-grained approach adjustments.

sections.heading: Conclusions and what comes next
sections.summary: This study formalized initial-pose dependence in dual-arm humanoid VLAs as a hand prior and demonstrated that localized arm joint angles serve as causal triggers for hand selection. The findings show that initial-pose diversification and targeted data augmentation in weak regions are effective, while emphasizing the importance of maintaining target data ratios during multi-task training.
sections.details:
This paper investigated the mechanisms by which initial pose distorts policy decision-making in humanoid dual-arm manipulation. Using the proposed HandPriorScore, the authors successfully detected asymmetric hand biases concealed behind average task success rates.

Intervention experiments confirmed that while wrist-camera visual cues aid fine adjustments, the root cause of inappropriate hand selection lies in specific right-arm joint angles ($R_{\mathrm{arm},3}$ and $R_{\mathrm{arm},5}$). Furthermore, the authors demonstrated that avoiding rigid coupling between initial poses and target positions during collection, densely covering failure-prone initial state neighborhoods, and maintaining sufficient target task exposure when mixing external data are key to achieving initial-pose robustness.

These findings strongly argue that explicitly designing initial-pose variations in both dataset collection and evaluation protocols is indispensable when deploying VLAs to dual-arm robotic systems.

takeaways: Do not rely solely on aggregate benchmark success rates; always examine performance variation and hand-selection skew across initial poses using metrics like HandPriorScore.

Avoid creating implicit couplings during data collection (e.g., always manipulating left-side objects from leftward initial poses), as policies will learn initial configurations as shortcuts over visual cues.
When facing low-performing initial poses, localized augmentation by adding a small amount of demonstration data near that configuration (identifiable in PCA space) is highly effective.
When co-training with heterogeneous robot or auxiliary task datasets, adjust resampling weights carefully so the sampling ratio of the target task is not overly diluted.
limitations: Evaluations are limited to a single task (PickApple), a single robot hardware platform (Unitree G1), and a single policy foundation (GR00T).
In joint-level intervention experiments, certain combinations resulted in kinematically infeasible poses, leading to small and non-uniform sample sizes in some conditions.
The wrist-camera masking analysis generates out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs, precluding a complete quantification of exact causal contribution ratios.
